0.title: The Letter of Jude: Contend for the Faith
0.overview:
Jude is one of the most neglected letters in the New Testament. Most Christians know the doxology at the end — and it is magnificent — but could not tell you what comes before it. What comes before it is some of the most urgent, vivid, and pastorally charged writing in the entire canon. Jude is a fire-bell.

The author identifies himself as “a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). He does not say “brother of the Lord” — though he almost certainly was. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 name “Judas” among the brothers of Jesus, and James was the recognized head of the Jerusalem church. Jude had credentials that would have opened every door in the early Christian world: raised in the same household as the Son of God, converted after the resurrection, brother to the most respected Jewish-Christian leader of the first generation. He uses none of it. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. The biological relationship, once the most important fact about him, has been swallowed up by a greater reality: the resurrection has changed the category. He no longer has a brother who happens to be the Messiah; he has a Lord who happens to have been his brother.

The occasion for the letter is stated plainly in v. 3. Jude had intended to write about “our common salvation” — a warm, constructive letter celebrating the faith they shared. He never wrote it. The crisis was too pressing. False teachers had “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4), and Jude found himself writing an alarm instead of a celebration. The letter we have is not the letter he planned. This matters pastorally: faithful ministry sometimes means setting aside what we intended to say in order to say what the moment requires.

The letter is twenty-five verses. It has no chapter breaks. It is a single sustained argument that moves from the alarm (vv. 3–4), through the evidence (vv. 5–16), to the counter-strategy for the faithful (vv. 17–23), and finally to one of the greatest doxologies in Scripture (vv. 24–25). The fire and the doxology belong together. The letter that begins with danger ends with adoration — and the adoration is not escapism. It is the theological ground on which the whole letter stands. You can contend for the faith without bitterness, rescue others without losing yourself, hold on under pressure — because the One who keeps you is infinitely more powerful than everything that threatens you.

1.title: Contend, Hold Fast, Adore
1.overview:
The single chapter of Jude moves in four distinct movements, each essential to the letter’s argument. First, Jude states his reason for writing: contend earnestly for the faith, because false teachers have secretly entered the community (vv. 3–4). Second, he marshals the evidence — three historical examples of judgment on those who had privilege and squandered it (vv. 5–7), followed by a blistering portrait of the false teachers who are now repeating those patterns (vv. 8–16). Third, the letter turns to the faithful: remember the apostles’ warnings, build yourselves up, stay in the love of God, and rescue those who are wavering (vv. 17–23). Fourth, the doxology: to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling, all glory (vv. 24–25).

The structure is pastorally brilliant. Jude does not end with the catalogue of judgment, though that catalogue is real and sobering. He ends with God. The darkness of vv. 5–16 is meant to be read in the light of vv. 24–25. The people who are being warned about false teachers are also the people who are called, beloved in God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ (v. 1). The letter holds the danger and the security together — not to create complacency, but to create a specific kind of courage: the courage of people who know they are held.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude’s opening three words for his recipients — called, beloved, kept — form a compressed theology of perseverance. Before a single argument is made, before the alarm is sounded, the congregation is told who they are. They were called (past action: God summoned them). They are beloved in God the Father (present reality: they rest in the Father’s love). They are kept for Jesus Christ (ongoing and future: maintained, guarded, preserved for the day of his appearing). These three words mean that the letter’s warning cannot end in despair. The people who need to hear about false teachers are the same people who are being kept by God.
verseByVerse.theology: The address “to those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ” is a miniature of the doctrine of election and perseverance. The passive verbs are significant: the recipients did not call themselves, do not sustain their own belovedness, and are not keeping themselves. All three realities are done to them and for them by God. This is the foundation of Jude’s pastoral strategy: he warns with urgency because the danger is real, but he addresses people who are divinely held. Reformed theology insists that these are not in tension. The warnings are the means by which the kept are kept; the keeping is the reason the warnings can be heard without despair.
verseByVerse.examples: The greeting sets the pastoral key for the whole letter. A preacher who only sounds the alarm — who only catalogues the dangers of false teaching and the judgment of the ungodly — without first telling people who they are in Christ will produce anxiety rather than faithfulness. Jude knows his people are beloved and kept before he tells them what is threatening them. Then: a congregation in the first century living in the middle of doctrinal crisis. Now: any believer who wonders whether the pressures of a post-Christian culture or the confusion of false teaching inside the church might finally overwhelm them. Jude’s opening words answer the question before it is asked: you are kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, To those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘A servant of Jesus Christ’ — the Greek is doulos: bond-slave, one whose will belongs to another. Jude could have written “brother of the Lord” and silenced every critic in the room. He had the biological credential no other NT author possessed. He chose not to use it. This is not false modesty; it is theology. The resurrection changed everything. Before Easter, Jude had a brother who was becoming increasingly difficult to explain. After Easter, he had a Lord. The most intimate human relationship in his life was now secondary to the covenant relationship that the resurrection had made possible. When Jude calls himself a doulos of Jesus, he is confessing that Easter happened and that it reordered everything.

‘Brother of James’ — he appeals to James not to claim status but to establish identity. The readers would have known James, the pillar of the Jerusalem church (Gal 2:9), and would have trusted any letter from his household. This is the credential Jude does use — not his biological proximity to Jesus but his connection to the leader the community already knew and trusted.

‘Called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ’ — three participial descriptions, each doing theological work. Called: the divine summons that brought them to faith; this is God’s act, not their initiative. Beloved in God the Father: loved not merely by the Father but loved “in” him — held within the sphere of his love, which is the only love that is unconditional and permanent. Kept: the Greek tēreō means to guard, to watch over, to maintain. They are not maintaining themselves; they are being maintained. These three words together are the foundation on which the entire letter’s argument rests: the people being warned are divinely held.

The greeting “mercy, peace, and love” is distinctive — slightly different from Paul’s standard “grace and peace.” The addition of “mercy” and “love” frames the letter in what God gives. In a letter about the danger of false teaching and the urgency of contending, Jude opens with what God provides to his people: mercy that does not hold their failures against them, peace that passes all understanding, and love that holds them no matter what.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter changes gear sharply at v. 3. The phrase “I found it necessary” carries the force of a sudden obligation pressing itself upon Jude from outside — a crisis that would not allow the letter he planned. This is worth holding: pastoral faithfulness sometimes means writing the letter the moment requires rather than the letter you preferred. The result is one of the most important single sentences in the New Testament for understanding how the church is to relate to its own doctrinal foundation: “contend earnestly for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.”
verseByVerse.theology:
“The faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (v. 3) is one of the NT’s clearest statements about the nature and finality of the apostolic gospel. Hapax — once, once for all, in a decisive and unrepeatable event — the faith was delivered in the apostolic period. It is not an evolving tradition that each generation renegotiates. It is not a seed that grows into something different from what was planted. It is a trust, a deposit, a fixed inheritance. The church receives it, guards it, and passes it on. No generation has the authority to alter what was once for all delivered. This is the theological basis for the Reformation’s appeal to Scripture: sola Scriptura means the faith delivered to the apostles is the norming norm, not the tradition of any particular century.

The false teachers of v. 4 are described with two charges. First, they “pervert the grace of our God into sensuality.” The most glorious truth of the gospel — that God justifies the ungodly by grace through faith — becomes in their hands a permission slip for immorality. Paul confronted the same logic in Romans 6 (“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”). Second, they “deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.” The denial is not necessarily verbal; they may still use his name. But a lifestyle that perverts grace is a practical denial of his Lordship. Jesus himself warned: “Not everyone who says to me ‘Lord, Lord’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.” Antinomianism is always, in the end, a Christological problem.
verseByVerse.examples: The word translated “contend earnestly” (v. 3) is a single compound Greek verb, epagōnizesthai, built on the root agōn — the athletic contest. We get the English word “agony” from the same root. This is not a casual engagement with ideas; it is the full-body effort of an athlete in a competition that costs something. The faith is not maintained without effort. Then: a first-century congregation infiltrated by teachers whose gracious-sounding theology was quietly destroying people. Now: a church in any century navigating the pressure to accommodate its doctrine to the surrounding culture. The questions change; the call to contend does not. What does “contend” look like? Not bitterness, not point-scoring, not the pleasure of being right. It looks like the effort of someone who loves the people who are being misled — which is why the same letter that calls for contending also calls for rescuing (vv. 22–23).

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, although I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation, I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘I was very eager to write to you about our common salvation’ — the intended letter was never written. A celebratory letter about the faith they all shared gave way to something harder and more urgent. The preacher should not pass over this: we learn something about Jude’s character from the letter he wanted to write and couldn’t. He is not a controversialist who enjoys a fight; he is a pastor who would have preferred to celebrate but found the situation demanded something else. It is the people who love the gospel most who find it hardest to watch it being distorted.

‘Certain people have crept in unnoticed’ — the Greek verb suggests slipping in alongside, entering by a side door. They were not announced; they did not come in openly. They came in the way that dangerous teaching almost always comes: gradually, plausibly, using the church’s own language. The most dangerous false teaching is not the kind that is obviously alien; it is the kind that sounds like the gospel while quietly removing its foundations.

‘Who long ago were designated for this condemnation’ — a statement about divine foreknowledge and sovereignty. God’s condemnation of the ungodly is not a reactive improvisation; the judgment of those who pervert his grace was written into the pattern of history from the beginning. This does not excuse their sin; it frames their story within God’s larger governance of all things.

‘Pervert the grace of our God into sensuality’ — the word “pervert” means to transpose, to change into something else. They have taken grace — the most radical, most beautiful, most transformative reality in the universe — and turned it into a moral blank check. This is not merely an ethical failure; it is a theological one. A grace that permits anything is not the grace of the NT, which “trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” (Tit 2:12). Any theology that produces licentiousness rather than holiness has not understood grace; it has replaced it with something that wears grace’s clothing.

‘Deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ’ — the denial may or may not be verbal. To claim his name while living as though his Lordship makes no claims on the body is to deny him in practice. Jude’s two charges are not separate: the perversion of grace and the denial of the Lord are two aspects of a single failure. A Christ who does not reign over the moral life is not the Christ of the NT. The Lordship of Jesus is not a theological abstraction; it is a claim on how we live.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude reaches for three examples from Israel’s scripture and tradition to make a single point: God judges the ungodly, and the pattern of that judgment has already been demonstrated in history. The three cases — Israel in the wilderness (v. 5), the fallen angels (v. 6), and Sodom and Gomorrah (v. 7) — share a structural logic: privilege, rebellion, judgment. These were not people on the margins who had no access to God. Israel was redeemed out of Egypt by miraculous power. The angels were the highest order of created beings. Sodom had the witness of righteous Lot in its midst. Each had extraordinary exposure to God’s grace; each turned that grace into permission for something God forbade; each was judged. The pattern is not accidental. And the pattern is being repeated in Jude’s day.
verseByVerse.theology:
The three examples establish a Reformed understanding of divine judgment that is both historical and eschatological. God’s judgments in history — the wilderness deaths, the chained angels, the fire on Sodom — are not isolated episodes but anticipations of the final judgment. This is why Jude describes Sodom’s punishment as “a punishment of eternal fire” (v. 7): the historical fire was a specimen, a deposit, a pledge of the fire that is to come. The same God who brought these judgments will bring the final one. This theological framework rules out the comfortable assumption that God’s patience means God’s indifference. His patience is real; his judgment is also real. The two belong together in the same God.

The example of Israel in v. 5 raises a significant textual question: the best Greek manuscripts read “Jesus” (Iēsous) rather than “the Lord” as the agent of the Exodus. If the earliest reading is “Jesus,” Jude is identifying the pre-incarnate Christ as the divine agent who both saved Israel from Egypt and afterward destroyed those who did not believe. This is consistent with Paul’s identification of Christ as the rock that followed Israel in the wilderness (1 Cor 10:4). The Christological implication is significant: the Christ who redeems is also the Christ who judges; there is no version of Jesus who saves without also holding accountable.
verseByVerse.examples: The structural logic of the three examples — privilege plus rebellion equals judgment — is one of the most searching theological patterns in Scripture. The most dangerous position is not ignorance of God but proximity to God without submission to him. Israel had seen the plagues and the parting of the sea. The angels had been before the throne. Sodom had a righteous man in its midst. None of it was sufficient without the response of faith and obedience. The application presses on every church: the people at greatest risk of the judgment Jude describes are not those who have never heard the gospel but those who have heard it and treated it as background noise. Greater privilege means greater accountability (Luke 12:48). The safest response to knowing the God of the Exodus, the God of creation, the God who sent Lot to Sodom, is not familiarity. It is worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I want to remind you, although you once fully knew it, that Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority, but left their proper dwelling, he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day — just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities, which likewise indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire, serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt’ (v. 5) — the textual question here is one of the most fascinating in Jude: the earliest and best Greek manuscripts read “Jesus” (Iēsous), while others read “the Lord” or “God.” Most modern critical editions accept “Jesus” as the original, precisely because it is the harder reading — scribes were more likely to smooth it to “the Lord” than to introduce “Jesus” into an OT context. If original, this is a bold piece of pre-incarnate Christology: the same Jesus who became flesh in Bethlehem was the divine agent of the Exodus from Egypt. Paul makes the same identification in 1 Corinthians 10:4, where the rock that followed Israel in the wilderness “was Christ.” In either reading, the theological point is identical: God — the same God who redeemed Israel — afterward destroyed those who did not believe. Salvation and judgment belong to the same Lord.

‘Afterward destroyed those who did not believe’ — Numbers 14 records the pivotal moment: Israel heard the report of the twelve spies, believed the ten who said they could not take the land, and in doing so refused to trust the God who had brought them out of Egypt with signs and wonders. The entire generation over twenty years old died in the wilderness. This is the event Jude cites. The same people whom God redeemed from Egypt perished for unbelief. The redemption did not insulate them from judgment when they refused faith. This is the first example’s warning: no historical privilege — no Exodus, no baptism, no church membership — substitutes for persevering faith.

‘The angels who did not stay within their own position of authority’ (v. 6) — the background is Genesis 6:1–4 and the tradition developed in 1 Enoch and other Jewish texts: angels who abandoned their proper station and pursued what was forbidden. These were the highest order of created beings — beings of glory and power who stood before the throne of God — and they left their assigned place. The consequence: “he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness until the judgment of the great day.” The contrast between their former dignity and their present condition is total. From the presence of God to eternal chains in gloomy darkness. Their position did not protect them; it made their fall more dramatic. The second example’s warning: authority and status are not shields against accountability. They are responsibilities that increase it.

‘Sodom and Gomorrah... serve as an example’ (v. 7) — the word deigma means an example, a specimen, a display-sample. The cities of the plain did not merely face judgment; they became an exhibit, a permanent warning-sign in the landscape of sacred history. Sodom had Abraham’s nephew Lot living in its midst — a “righteous man” (2 Pet 2:7) whose daily presence was a silent witness to a better way. They rejected it. The fire that fell on them was not the final fire; it was a foretaste of it, a pledge of what the Judge of all the earth will do when the day of the great judgment arrives. The fire on the plain of Jordan was a sample. The real fire is still coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The False Teachers: A Portrait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having established the historical pattern, Jude turns to the false teachers themselves. What he gives is not a careful doctrinal analysis but a vivid, almost overwhelming portrait — image after image, analogy after analogy — of people who have the form of Christian community but are destroying it from within. The images accumulate deliberately: waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. Each one describes a teacher who creates the expectation of nourishment and then delivers nothing — or worse, delivers harm.
verseByVerse.theology: The Michael and the devil episode in v. 9 is one of the most theologically rich details in Jude. Even the archangel Michael — the commander of the heavenly host, a being of incomparably greater dignity and power than any human teacher — did not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against Satan by his own authority. He said: “The Lord rebuke you.” He deferred the judgment to God. The false teachers, by contrast, “blaspheme whatever they do not understand” (v. 10) and speak contemptuously of the “glorious ones” — almost certainly the angelic powers that administer the moral order of creation. The contrast is devastating: the creature of greatest power deferred; the creatures of least understanding presume. Contempt for divine order, for the structures of God’s governance, is not sophistication. It is an arrogance that surpasses even the angels who fell.
verseByVerse.examples: The six images of vv. 12–13 form one of the most concentrated passages of sustained metaphor in the NT, and the preacher should not hurry past them. Waterless clouds — all the appearance of refreshment, none of the substance. Fruitless trees in late autumn — the season when fruit should be there and is not; and “twice dead” because they were once offered life and refused it, deepening their deadness. Wild waves — all noise and movement, producing nothing but refuse at the shoreline. Wandering stars — this is perhaps the most haunting: stars that wander from their fixed courses are useless for navigation. A teacher who cannot be trusted to hold the truth is not neutral; he actively misleads those who are trying to find their way. These images are not emotional excess; they are precise theological description. What makes the false teacher dangerous is not his power but his pretense: he looks like what is needed and is not it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in like manner these people also, relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones. But when the archangel Michael, contending with the devil, was disputing about the body of Moses, he did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you.' But these people blaspheme all that they do not understand, and they are destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively. Woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain and abandoned themselves for the sake of gain to Balaam’s error and perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are hidden reefs at your love feasts, as they feast with you without fear, shepherds feeding themselves; waterless clouds, swept along by winds; fruitless trees in late autumn, without fruit, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Relying on their dreams’ (v. 8) — the first detail about the false teachers’ self-understanding. They claim direct revelatory experience — visions, dreams — that authorize their behavior. This is the ancient form of an appeal that has never gone away: “God told me directly” as justification for setting aside what God has revealed publicly and permanently. The appeal to private revelation as a license for moral departure from the apostolic faith is not a modern invention; Jude was already dealing with it in the first generation.

Three charges follow: they “defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones.” These correspond to the three examples of vv. 5–7: Sodom defiled the flesh; the fallen angels rejected their assigned authority; Israel blasphemed God’s appointed representatives. The false teachers are reenacting all three patterns simultaneously.

The Michael episode (v. 9) — not recorded in the OT, but drawn from a Jewish tradition (possibly the Assumption of Moses) — gives Jude the most devastating comparison available. Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not say “I condemn you” or “Be gone, you rebel.” He said: “The Lord rebuke you.” The judgment belongs to God; even the archangel will not usurp it. Now set that alongside the false teachers who blaspheme what they do not understand, who speak with contemptuous confidence about things that exceed their knowledge. Michael, with infinitely more authority and understanding than these teachers, showed infinitely more restraint. The comparison is not subtle. It is meant to expose the false teachers’ presumption as the absurdity it is.

Verse 11 — the threefold “Woe” pattern: Cain, Balaam, and Korah. Cain represents the spiritual envy that leads to violence against a brother — religious murder growing out of self-will and jealousy. Balaam represents the prostitution of a genuine spiritual gift in service of financial reward — the prophet who loved the wages of unrighteousness and repeatedly attempted to curse Israel for payment from Balak (Num 22–24). Korah represents rebellion against divinely appointed leadership — the man who led a revolt against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth (Num 16). Three OT cases, three patterns of spiritual failure — and the false teachers are walking in all three. The “Woe” is not an epithet; it is prophetic judicial language, the same “Woe” Jesus pronounces in Matthew 23.

The six images of vv. 12–13: Hidden reefs at your love feasts — the love feast was the church’s communal meal accompanying the Lord’s Supper; these teachers attend “without fear,” eating the community’s food and sharing its fellowship while destroying it from within. Shepherds feeding themselves — the precise inversion of the pastoral calling (Ezek 34:2–4): shepherds exist to feed the flock, not to feed from it. Waterless clouds — in a Mediterranean climate, clouds on the horizon meant hope of rain; waterless clouds are deception made visible. Fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted — autumn is when fruit should be there and is not; “twice dead” because they were once offered life by the gospel and refused it, compounding their original deadness; “uprooted” because their end is complete removal. Wild waves casting up foam — all turbulent energy, no nourishment, only refuse at the shore. Wandering stars — the most haunting image: a star that wanders from its fixed position in the night sky is useless and dangerous for navigation. The teacher who cannot be trusted to hold the apostolic faith does not merely fail to guide — he actively misleads those trying to find the way. And for such stars: “the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jude quotes from 1 Enoch 1:9, a Jewish apocalyptic text written centuries before Christ and widely read in the first-century Jewish world. He attributes the words to “Enoch, the seventh from Adam” (v. 14) — the Enoch of Genesis 5:21–24 who “walked with God and was not, for God took him.” This raises a question that preachers will face: how can an inspired NT author quote a non-canonical source as if it carries prophetic weight? The answer is that Jude does not say “the Scripture says” but “Enoch prophesied.” He can affirm that a true statement in 1 Enoch is genuinely prophetic without canonizing the whole book. The content of the prophecy — the Lord coming with myriads of his holy ones to execute judgment — is entirely consistent with the rest of Scripture (Zech 14:5; Dan 7:10; Matt 25:31; Rev 19:14). Jude is affirming what is true, not endorsing the authority of his source.
verseByVerse.theology: The Enoch prophecy focuses on the certainty and comprehensiveness of divine judgment. “To execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness… and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him” (vv. 14–15). The fourfold repetition of “ungodly” (asebeis, asebeia, asebōs, asebeis) is emphatic and deliberate: it characterizes not just the acts but the persons, not just the deeds but the words, not just the words but the disposition behind them. The judgment of God is not merely behavioral; it reaches to the heart. Every hidden motive, every contemptuous word, every act that may have passed unnoticed in the human community — all of it will be brought into the open. This is not a God who grades on a curve.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 16 closes the portrait with three further characteristics: the false teachers are “grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires” and they “show favoritism to gain advantage.” This last detail is particularly sharp: they flatter people. Their community relationships are instrumental — they say what people want to hear in order to get what they want from them. This is the opposite of the pastoral relationship Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 2:3–6, where he refuses flattery precisely because he has been entrusted with the gospel. The false teacher who flatters is not loving his congregation; he is using it. The contrast with genuine pastoral care could not be sharper: the true shepherd tells people what they need to hear even when it is hard. The false teacher tells people what they want to hear because he needs something from them.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.' These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires; they are loud-mouthed boasters, showing favoritism to gain advantage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘Enoch, the seventh from Adam’ — the designation “seventh from Adam” comes from 1 Enoch itself and establishes Enoch’s antiquity and closeness to the beginning. The Enoch of Genesis walked with God (5:22, 24) and was taken by God without dying — one of only two people in Scripture of whom this is said (Elijah is the other). Jewish tradition had elaborated extensively on this figure; 1 Enoch was perhaps the most widely read Jewish apocalyptic text of the NT period. Jude cites it here not as Scripture but as containing a genuine prophetic statement about the coming judgment. Paul does something similar in Acts 17:28 (quoting the Greek poet Aratus) and Titus 1:12 (quoting Epimenides of Crete): a true statement is true regardless of its literary source.

‘The Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones’ — the imagery of divine judgment accompanied by a vast heavenly retinue runs through the OT (Deut 33:2; Dan 7:10; Zech 14:5) and is carried through the NT (Matt 25:31; 2 Thess 1:7; Rev 19:14). The sheer number — “ten thousands” is a Greek number suggesting an uncountable multitude — is meant to communicate the overwhelming, irresistible nature of the coming judgment. There is no defense against it, no appeal from it, no escape from it. When that day comes, the false teachers’ bluster will be entirely silent.

‘To execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds” — the fourfold “all” combined with the fourfold “ungodly” means the judgment is comprehensive in both scope (all people, all deeds) and in target (the ungodly in their ungodliness). Nothing is overlooked; nothing is excused; nothing that was hidden will remain hidden. The word “convict” here is legal — to demonstrate guilt conclusively before a court. This is not an emotional accusation but a judicial finding. The ungodly will not merely be condemned; they will be shown to be condemned, their guilt made undeniable even to themselves.

Verses 15–16 close the portrait of the false teachers by describing them in their daily social behavior: grumblers, malcontents, following sinful desires, loud-mouthed boasters, flatterers. The detail about flattery is especially revealing. These teachers cultivated relationships of apparent admiration in order to extract what they wanted. They said what their audience wanted to hear — and their audience paid them for it. It is the oldest and most seductive form of false ministry: telling people what they want to hear, gaining influence, and using that influence for personal benefit. The congregation that feeds this kind of teacher, that rewards flattery with loyalty, is being used by people who do not love them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–23 — Hold Fast: The Call to the Faithful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter turns at v. 17 with one of the most pastorally significant words in the passage: “But you, beloved.” For twelve verses the congregation has been hearing about the false teachers — described in the third person, painted in the darkest colors. Now Jude turns directly to the people he loves and calls them “beloved.” The tone shifts from indictment to instruction. The portrait of the enemy is finished; now comes the counter-strategy of the faithful. And the counter-strategy is not primarily defensive or reactive — it is about what the faithful community is to be in itself, and then what it is to do for those on the margins who are in danger.
verseByVerse.theology:
The four-fold call of vv. 20–21 — building, praying, keeping, waiting — describes the shape of a life that does not capitulate to false teaching without becoming brittle or fearful. These are not emergency measures for a church under siege; they are the marks of a community that is genuinely alive. They build on the most holy faith; they pray in the Holy Spirit; they keep themselves in the love of God; they wait for the mercy of Christ. The Trinitarian structure is striking: the Spirit-empowered prayer, the keeping within the Father’s love, and the waiting for the Son’s appearing. The entire life of the faithful community is framed by and sustained by the Trinity.

The rescue mission of vv. 22–23 is one of the most careful pastoral instructions in the NT regarding how to engage with those who are wavering or have strayed. Three categories are distinguished: those who doubt (treat with mercy and patience); those in urgent danger (“snatch them out of the fire” — the urgency of someone pulling a person from a burning building); and those so deeply compromised that even the rescue must be carried out with extreme caution (“show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by sin”). Jude does not call for wholesale withdrawal from the endangered. He calls for differentiated, wise engagement — but engagement nonetheless.
verseByVerse.examples: ‘Keep yourselves in the love of God’ (v. 21) — this command is often misread as an instruction to generate or maintain warm feelings toward God, which would be an exhausting and uncertain enterprise. But “keep yourselves in the love of God” means: remain within the sphere of his love. God’s love is the environment of the Christian life; the call is to stay in it, not to step outside it. The call to obedience, to prayer, to community, to perseverance in faith — these are not the ways we earn God’s love. They are the ways we remain consciously within the love that already surrounds us and holds us. Then: a church in the first century pressed from within by teachers who were pulling people away from the apostolic faith. Now: the believer who is tempted to drift from the community of faith, from the practices of prayer and Scripture and worship, toward something that feels easier or more culturally comfortable. The call is the same: stay in the love of God. It is the safest place in the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: But you must remember, beloved, the predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you, 'In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.' It is these who cause divisions, worldly people, devoid of the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘But you, beloved, must remember’ — the sudden turn in address marks the letter’s pivot. For several verses the false teachers have been held up in the light, their corruption exposed. Now Jude speaks directly to the people he loves. “Beloved” — this is who they are to him, regardless of the crisis. The pastoral relationship survives the alarm.

‘The predictions of the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ’ — Jude points back to apostolic prophecy about end-time false teachers. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that after his departure “fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock” (Acts 20:29–30). He told Timothy that “in later times some will depart from the faith” (1 Tim 4:1). Peter described the scoffers who would deny the Lord’s return (2 Pet 3:3). The crisis Jude’s congregation is facing is not a surprise; it is the predicted pattern of the last days. This matters pastorally: the person who knows that false teaching was promised is less likely to be disoriented when it arrives. The map includes the difficulty. We are not lost.

‘In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions’ — the apostolic description of the false teachers is identical to Jude’s. Their theology serves their lifestyle. They have not arrived at their theological conclusions by honest inquiry and found that the conclusions happen to free them from moral constraint; they have decided what they want to do and then constructed a theology to justify it. This is the fundamental pattern of all antinomian theology in every generation: the ethics come first, the doctrine follows to legitimize them.

‘Devoid of the Spirit’ (v. 19) — the Greek word is psychikoi: natural, soulish, living at the level of the unregenerate human nature. This is the most devastating thing Jude can say about the false teachers — and he says it last in the portrait, for maximum effect. All their claims to special spiritual experience, all their appeals to dreams and visions and direct revelation, and they do not have the Spirit. The one thing they most loudly claim to possess is the one thing they most conspicuously lack. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. The fruit of the false teachers is division, licentiousness, grumbling, and self-promotion. The tree is known by its fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, beloved, building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life. And have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire; to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 20–21 cluster four present-tense participles around the central imperative “keep yourselves in the love of God.” The grammar is important: the keeping is the command; the four activities are the means. Building yourselves up in your most holy faith — not a passive reception of instruction but an active construction, a deliberate building of the communal life on the foundation of the apostolic faith. The faith is called “most holy” — the superlative of holiness applied not to a behavior but to a body of belief. The faith itself is sacred; it is set apart, it is the Lord’s. Treating it carelessly is a form of sacrilege. Praying in the Holy Spirit — prayer that is not merely human effort but Spirit-enabled communion; the Spirit intercedes for us (Rom 8:26–27), and prayer “in the Spirit” means coming into alignment with the Spirit’s own intercession. Waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life — the horizon of the Christian life is not the end of this age but the mercy of Christ at his appearing; the “mercy” here is the same mercy Jude opened with in v. 2, the mercy multiplied to the faithful. They have received mercy; they are waiting for more of it, the final and fullest form of it, when Christ comes.

The rescue mission of vv. 22–23 is the most nuanced pastoral instruction in the letter. Three categories of the endangered are described, each requiring a different approach. The doubters (v. 22) need patient mercy — these are not the committed false teachers but people who have been unsettled by the false teaching, whose faith has been disturbed, who are genuinely uncertain. They need compassion, not condemnation. The urgently endangered (v. 23a) need active rescue — “snatch them out of the fire” uses the language of emergency intervention, as if someone were already inside a burning building. There is no time for lengthy discussion; they must be pulled out. And the deeply compromised (v. 23b) must be approached with extreme caution: mercy, yes, but “with fear, hating even the garment stained by sin.” The image is of a rescuer who must enter a contaminated environment — the rescue is not cancelled, but the rescuer must be careful not to be contaminated in the process.

This three-fold pattern is one of the most practically wise pieces of pastoral instruction in the NT. The same approach does not work for everyone. The person gently wavering needs gentle mercy. The person rapidly falling needs urgent intervention. The person deeply enmeshed in the false system needs a rescuer who is both merciful and self-protected. The preacher who learns these distinctions will be a better shepherd.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter that began with alarm ends with adoration. This is not a sentimental addition stitched onto the end of a serious letter; it is the theological ground on which the whole letter stands. Jude has been writing about stumbling — false teachers who have stumbled and are causing others to stumble, examples of those who fell catastrophically in the wilderness, in the heavens, in the cities of the plain. And now he lifts his eyes — and his congregation’s eyes — to the One who is able to keep them from stumbling. The doxology answers the letter. It is not an afterthought; it is the resolution. The letter can only be read rightly if it is read all the way to the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
Every word of the doxology carries doctrinal weight. “Him who is able” — the omnipotence of God is pledged to the preservation of his people. This is not a pious hope; it is a theological claim about what God can do. “To keep you from stumbling” — the Greek word aptaistos appears only here in the NT: unstumbling, without a fall. The God who keeps does not merely prevent catastrophic apostasy; he keeps his people from the stumbles that would otherwise accumulate into a fall. “To present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” — the destination of the keeping is the presence of God’s glory. The word “present” (histēmi) is the language of formal presentation before a king or court. The kept ones are not merely admitted; they are escorted and formally presented. And the presentation happens “with great joy” (en agalliasei) — exultation, triumphant delight. The God who keeps does not grudgingly maintain his people and then barely usher them through. He presents them before his own glory with exultation.

The doxology closes with the cascade of divine attributes: “glory, majesty, dominion, and authority.” And the time frame: “before all time and now and forever.” The glory of God was not given to him at some point in history; it belongs to him before time began. It belongs to him now, in the middle of a world where false teachers are undermining faith and faithful people are struggling to hold on. It will belong to him when the last enemy is destroyed and the new creation is the home of righteousness. The letter began with a crisis. It ends with an eternal God who holds all of history — including the crisis — within the reach of his glory, majesty, dominion, and authority. This is the ground on which the contending is possible. This is the reason the kept can sleep.
verseByVerse.examples: The doxology is meant to be felt, not merely analyzed. The preacher who has faithfully worked through the letter — the crept-in teachers, the three examples of judgment, the portrait of false teachers as wandering stars, the call to contend — arrives here and finds the answer to every anxiety the letter has raised. Can we hold on? The One who is able to keep you holds you. Will we be found acceptable? He will present you blameless before the presence of his glory. Will the false teachers finally win? To the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. He was sovereign before the crisis. He is sovereign in it. He will be sovereign after it. The doxology is not an escape from the letter’s realism; it is the foundation on which the realism can be faced without despair. Charles Spurgeon, preaching on this passage, said it was the kind of verse a man could die on. He was right.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘To him who is able’ — the opening phrase of the doxology is not a rhetorical flourish but a theological declaration. God is not merely willing to keep his people; he is able. The omnipotence of God is the first thing Jude says about him in the doxology. In a letter about the danger of falling, about the examples of those who did fall — Israel, the angels, Sodom — this is the answer that reframes everything. The stumbling you fear, the ground you might lose, the false teaching that might overwhelm you: the One who keeps you is the One who spoke creation into existence and holds it together by the word of his power. His ability to keep is not in question.

‘To keep you from stumbling’ — the Greek word (aptaistos) means unstumbling, without a fall, and appears nowhere else in the NT. It is a word Jude has apparently coined or selected for this exact moment — the final word about what God does for his people in a letter that has been saturated with examples of those who stumbled and fell. The keeping is not passive; it is active and continuous. God is not a safety net at the bottom of the cliff; he is a shepherd on the path, preventing the stumbles that would lead to the fall.

‘To present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy’ — the verb “present” is the language of formal presentation to a person of supreme authority: a king, a court, a judge. The ones being kept are not merely admitted to the presence of glory; they are escorted, formally introduced, presented. And they are presented blameless — the Greek word amōmous is the term used for a sacrifice without defect, the animal that could be offered to God because it was without spot or blemish. Every believer who has ever felt the weight of their own failure, their own inadequacy, their own moral imperfection — this word is for them. They will be presented as a spotless offering. Not because they were, in themselves, without fault, but because the One who keeps them also cleanses them, and the One who presents them guarantees the presentation.

‘With great joy’ (en agalliasei) — the word is not quiet contentment or mild satisfaction. Agalliasis is exultation, leaping joy, the kind of joy that breaks out of ordinary expression. The God who keeps his people and presents them blameless does so with exultation. This is the joy of the father running to meet the prodigal (Luke 15:20). This is the joy of the shepherd finding the lost sheep (Luke 15:5). This is the joy that was set before Christ, for which he endured the cross (Heb 12:2). The kept ones will be presented before the glory of God with the exultation of the One who kept them. The homecoming of the saints is a joy to God.

‘The only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord’ — the Trinitarian structure of the doxology is clear: it is addressed to God the Father (“the only God”), mediated through Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit implied in the keeping and presenting (cf. v. 20, “praying in the Holy Spirit”). The title “our Savior” applied to the Father is unusual in the NT (more commonly applied to Jesus) but not unprecedented (cf. 1 Tim 1:1; 2:3; Titus 1:3; 2:10). The salvation accomplished by Christ is the salvation of God; the mediator and the one through whom he mediates share the same saving purpose.

‘Be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.’ — the four attributes cascade: glory (the weight and radiance of God’s own being, the kabod, the shekinah), majesty (the sovereign dignity that cannot be approached without reverence), dominion (the supreme exercise of rule over all created things), authority (the inherent right from which that dominion flows). And the time frame is total: before all time — before the creation, before the crisis in heaven, before the garden — he was glorious. Now — in the middle of the first century with false teachers in the church and the congregation struggling to hold on — he is glorious. Forever — when every enemy is defeated, every tear wiped away, every stumbler preserved and presented — he will be glorious. The letter that began with an alarm ends with the God who was never alarmed. He was sovereign before the crisis. He is sovereign in it. He will be sovereign on the other side of it. To him be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority. Amen.
